chunks: From him, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:
A gift (hiba) and a grant (nuhl) may be reclaimed by its owner if he wishes, whether it has been taken possession of or not, except for one of kinship, for indeed he does not reclaim it.

key_terms.الْهِبَةُ: Gift (a voluntary transfer of property without consideration)
key_terms.اَلنُّحْلُ: Grant (a type of gift or endowment, often used interchangeably with hiba in this context)
key_terms.حِيزَتْ: Taken possession of (perfected by taking hold)
key_terms.لِذِي رَحِمٍ: For one of kinship (referring to close relatives)
key_terms.يَرْجِعُ: To reclaim / to return (the right to take back the gift)

ai.seo_question: Can a gift be taken back after it has been given, and does kinship affect this right?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the general principle in Shia jurisprudence that a gift (hiba) is revocable by the donor unless it has been consumed or given to a close relative (dhawi rahm), reflecting the Prophetic tradition that 'a gift to a relative is not a gift but a replenishment of kinship.' The exception for relatives underscores the spiritual merit of maintaining family ties, distinguishing charitable kinship gifts from simple transfers of property. This ruling is foundational in the chapter on gifts within al-Tusi's Tahdhib al-Ahkam, illustrating the interplay between civil contract law and social ethics.
